newsitem.title: FRANCE: World price rally to hit French coffee drinkers.
newsitem.headline: World price rally to hit French coffee drinkers.

text.p: French consumers will soon have to pay more for a cup of coffee following soaring world prices, coffee firms warned on Thursday.
The warning came as already-high coffee prices surged again after producing countries agreed to extend cartel-style export quotas for 12 more months.
"By the end of June consumers will feel the impact of price increases passed onto the shops in April," said Jean-Claude Frankel, chairman of the French coffee industry association.
Some firms plan more rises, which should be felt in autumn. "It is very likely that consumption will fall in 1997," he said in an interview.
In New York on Wednesday July arabica coffee futures soared 12.85 cents per pound to end at 253.10 cents.

Concerns over tight supplies in Latin America and low stocks in consumer countries has also helped push prices higher. Similar worries forced French roasters to raise retail prices for top quality beans by as much as 45 percent since the year began.

Frankel said this could not come at a worse time for the coffee industry in France, where consumption had been slowly recovering after previous price increases drove demand down by seven percent in 1994-95. Demand rebounded three percent last year and was broadly stable in the first quarter of 1997.
Although roasters were anxious not to scare away consumers, price hikes could not be ruled out in the face of volatile futures markets, Frankel said.
French roasters, who operate with very tight stocks, have complained they were being held hostage by speculators who do not pay attention to the laws of supply and demand.

Some roasters expect prices of some top quality washed arabicas to stay high until year-end but other coffees prices to ease in the autumn, provided there are no problems in Brazil, where the frost season is fast approaching.
Leading French coffee roasters include Kraft Jacobs Suchard (KJS), part of Philip Morris and Douwe Egberts France, owned by Sara Lee Corp.
French Cafes Excella SA, a distributor brand that has a five percent market share, also announced retail price rises.

Part of Wednesday's surge in prices was triggered by forecasts of cold weather moving into Brazil later this week. No frost is expected yet in the number one producer's coffee regions, but traders remain jittery as winter begins.
In New York, where quality arabica beans grown in Latin America are traded, the July contract hit a 20-year high last week.

The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC), anxious to defend prices after the fever in the market abates, ended London talks on Wednesday with an accord to limit total exports by the 14 members to 52.75 million (60 kg) bags for the 12 months from July 1.
This is about the same as the current limit which expires on June 30. A statement said the goal was "to ensure prices remain at a level remunerative to producers".

Analysts say the ACPC is worried speculative funds could cash in their gains and send the market down again, particularly at the end of the Brazilian winter in about 15 weeks' time, if there is no frost to damage the crop.
